[§](https://docs.rs#crate-feature-flags)Crate Feature Flags

The following crate [feature flags](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section) are available:

-
A set of features controlling the [static verbosity level](https://docs.rs/level_filters/index.html#compile-time-filters).
-
`log`: causes trace instrumentation points to emit`log``tracing`subscriber has not been set. This is intended for use in libraries whose users may be using either`tracing`or`log`.
-
`log-always`: Emit`log`records from all`tracing`spans and events, even if a`tracing`subscriber has been set. This should be set only by applications which intend to collect traces and logs separately; if an adapter is used to convert`log`records into`tracing`events, this will cause duplicate events to occur.
-
`attributes`: Includes support for the`#[instrument]`attribute. This is on by default, but does bring in the`syn`crate as a dependency, which may add to the compile time of crates that do not already use it.
-
`std`: Depend on the Rust standard library (enabled by default).`no_std`users may disable this feature with`default-features = false`:`[dependencies] tracing = { version = "0.1.38", default-features = false }`

```

```
**Note**: `tracing`'s `no_std` support
     requires `liballoc`.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable Features

These feature flags enable **unstable** features. The public API may break in 0.1.x
releases. To enable these features, the `--cfg tracing_unstable` must be passed to
`rustc` when compiling.

The following unstable feature flags are currently available:

- `valuable`: Enables support for recording- [field values](https://docs.rs/field/index.html)using the- `valuable`

[§](https://docs.rs#enabling-unstable-features)Enabling Unstable Features

The easiest way to set the `tracing_unstable` cfg is to use the `RUSTFLAGS`
env variable when running `cargo` commands:

`RUSTFLAGS="--cfg tracing_unstable" cargo build`Alternatively, the following can be added to the `.cargo/config` file in a
project to automatically enable the cfg flag for that project:

```
[build]
rustflags = ["--cfg", "tracing_unstable"]
```
[§](https://docs.rs#supported-rust-versions)Supported Rust Versions

Tracing is built against the latest stable release. The minimum supported version is 1.65. The current Tracing version is not guaranteed to build on Rust versions earlier than the minimum supported version.

Tracing follows the same compiler support policies as the rest of the Tokio project. The current stable Rust compiler and the three most recent minor versions before it will always be supported. For example, if the current stable compiler version is 1.69, the minimum supported version will not be increased past 1.66, three minor versions prior. Increasing the minimum supported compiler version is not considered a semver breaking change as long as doing so complies with this policy.

# uuid - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/uuid/^1.8.0/

## Expand description

Generate and parse universally unique identifiers (UUIDs).

Here’s an example of a UUID:

`67e55044-10b1-426f-9247-bb680e5fe0c8`A UUID is a unique 128-bit value, stored as 16 octets, and regularly formatted as a hex string in five groups. UUIDs are used to assign unique identifiers to entities without requiring a central allocating authority.

They are particularly useful in distributed systems, though can be used in disparate areas, such as databases and network protocols. Typically a UUID is displayed in a readable string form as a sequence of hexadecimal digits, separated into groups by hyphens.

The uniqueness property is not strictly guaranteed, however for all practical purposes, it can be assumed that an unintentional collision would be extremely unlikely.

UUIDs have a number of standardized encodings that are specified in [RFC 9562](https://www.ietf.org/rfc/rfc9562.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#getting-started)Getting started

Add the following to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies.uuid]
version = "1.23.4"
# Lets you generate random UUIDs
features = [
    "v4",
]
```
When you want a UUID, you can generate one:

```
use uuid::Uuid;
let id = Uuid::new_v4();
```
If you have a UUID value, you can use its string literal form inline:

```
use uuid::{uuid, Uuid};
const ID: Uuid = uuid!("67e55044-10b1-426f-9247-bb680e5fe0c8");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#working-with-different-uuid-versions)Working with different UUID versions

This library supports all standardized methods for generating UUIDs through individual Cargo features.

By default, this crate depends on nothing but the Rust standard library and can parse and format UUIDs, but cannot generate them. Depending on the kind of UUID you’d like to work with, there are Cargo features that enable generating them:

- `v1`- Version 1 UUIDs using a timestamp and monotonic counter.
- `v3`- Version 3 UUIDs based on the MD5 hash of some data.
- `v4`- Version 4 UUIDs with random data.
- `v5`- Version 5 UUIDs based on the SHA1 hash of some data.
- `v6`- Version 6 UUIDs using a timestamp and monotonic counter.
- `v7`- Version 7 UUIDs using a Unix timestamp.
- `v8`- Version 8 UUIDs using user-defined data.

This library also includes a [ Builder](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html) type that can be used to help construct UUIDs of any
version without any additional dependencies or features. It’s a lower-level API than

[that can be used when you need control over implicit requirements on things like a source of randomness.](https://docs.rs/struct.Uuid.html)

`Uuid`[§](https://docs.rs#which-uuid-version-should-i-use)Which UUID version should I use?

If you just want to generate unique identifiers then consider version 4 (`v4`) UUIDs. If you want
to use UUIDs as database keys or need to sort them then consider version 7 (`v7`) UUIDs.
Other versions should generally be avoided unless there’s an existing need for them.

Some UUID versions supersede others. Prefer version 6 over version 1 and version 5 over version 3.

[§](https://docs.rs#other-features)Other features

Other crate features can also be useful beyond the version support:

- `serde`- adds the ability to serialize and deserialize a UUID using- `serde`.
- `borsh`- adds the ability to serialize and deserialize a UUID using- `borsh`.
- `arbitrary`- adds an- `Arbitrary`trait implementation to- `Uuid`for fuzzing.
- `fast-rng`- uses a faster algorithm for generating random UUIDs when available. This feature requires more dependencies to compile, but is just as suitable for UUIDs as the default algorithm.
- `rng-rand`- forces- `rand`as the backend for randomness.
- `rng-getrandom`- forces- `getrandom`as the backend for randomness.
- `bytemuck`- adds a- `Pod`trait implementation to- `Uuid`for byte manipulation

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

Some features are unstable. They may be incomplete or depend on other unstable libraries. These include:

- `zerocopy`- adds support for zero-copy deserialization using the- `zerocopy`library.

Unstable features may break between minor releases.

To allow unstable features, you’ll need to enable the Cargo feature as
normal, but also pass an additional flag through your environment to opt-in
to unstable `uuid` features:

`RUSTFLAGS="--cfg uuid_unstable"`[§](https://docs.rs#building-for-other-targets)Building for other targets

[§](https://docs.rs#webassembly)WebAssembly

For WebAssembly, enable the `js` feature:

```
[dependencies.uuid]
version = "1.23.4"
features = [
    "v4",
    "v7",
    "js",
]
```
[§](https://docs.rs#embedded)Embedded

For embedded targets without the standard library, you’ll need to
disable default features when building `uuid`:

```
[dependencies.uuid]
version = "1.23.4"
default-features = false
```
Some additional features are supported in no-std environments:

- `v1`,- `v3`,- `v5`,- `v6`, and- `v8`.
- `serde`.

If you need to use `v4` or `v7` in a no-std environment, you’ll need to
produce random bytes yourself and then pass them to [ Builder::from_random_bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.Builder.html#method.from_random_bytes)
without enabling the

`v4` or `v7` features.If you’re using `getrandom`, you can specify the `rng-getrandom` or `rng-rand`
features of `uuid` and configure `getrandom`’s provider per its docs. `uuid`
may upgrade its version of `getrandom` in minor releases.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Parse a UUID given in the simple format and print it as a URN:

```
let my_uuid = Uuid::parse_str("a1a2a3a4b1b2c1c2d1d2d3d4d5d6d7d8")?;
println!("{}", my_uuid.urn());
```
Generate a random UUID and print it out in hexadecimal form:

```
// Note that this requires the `v4` feature to be enabled.
let my_uuid = Uuid::new_v4();
println!("{}", my_uuid);
```

# x509_parser - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/x509-parser/^0.17.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#x509-parser)X.509 Parser

A X.509 v3 ([RFC5280](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc5280)) parser, implemented with the [nom](https://github.com/Geal/nom)
parser combinator framework.

It is written in pure Rust, fast, and makes extensive use of zero-copy. A lot of care is taken to ensure security and safety of this crate, including design (recursion limit, defensive programming), tests, and fuzzing. It also aims to be panic-free.

The code is available on [Github](https://github.com/rusticata/x509-parser)
and is part of the [Rusticata](https://github.com/rusticata) project.

Certificates are usually encoded in two main formats: PEM (usually the most common format) or
DER.  A PEM-encoded certificate is a container, storing a DER object. See the
[ pem](https://docs.rs/pem/index.html) module for more documentation.

To decode a DER-encoded certificate, the main parsing method is
`X509Certificate::from_der` (
part of the [ FromDer](https://docs.rs/prelude/trait.FromDer.html) trait
), which builds a

[object.](https://docs.rs/certificate/struct.X509Certificate.html)

`X509Certificate`An alternative method is to use [ X509CertificateParser](https://docs.rs/certificate/struct.X509CertificateParser.html),
which allows specifying parsing options (for example, not automatically parsing option contents).

The returned objects for parsers follow the definitions of the RFC. This means that accessing
fields is done by accessing struct members recursively. Some helper functions are provided, for
example [ X509Certificate::issuer()](https://docs.rs/certificate/struct.X509Certificate.html#method.issuer) returns the
same as accessing

`<object>.tbs_certificate.issuer`.For PEM-encoded certificates, use the [ pem](https://docs.rs/pem/index.html) module.

This crate also provides visitor traits: [ X509CertificateVisitor](https://docs.rs/visitor/trait.X509CertificateVisitor.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Parsing a certificate in DER format:

```
use x509_parser::prelude::*;
static IGCA_DER: &[u8] = include_bytes!("../assets/IGC_A.der");
let res = X509Certificate::from_der(IGCA_DER);
match res {
    Ok((rem, cert)) => {
        assert!(rem.is_empty());
        //
        assert_eq!(cert.version(), X509Version::V3);
    },
    _ => panic!("x509 parsing failed: {:?}", res),
}
```
To parse a CRL and print information about revoked certificates:

```
let res = CertificateRevocationList::from_der(DER);
match res {
    Ok((_rem, crl)) => {
        for revoked in crl.iter_revoked_certificates() {
            println!("Revoked certificate serial: {}", revoked.raw_serial_as_string());
            println!("  Reason: {}", revoked.reason_code().unwrap_or_default().1);
        }
    },
    _ => panic!("CRL parsing failed: {:?}", res),
}
```
See also `examples/print-cert.rs`.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- The `verify`feature adds support for (cryptographic) signature verification, based on`ring`. It adds the`X509Certificate::verify_signature()``X509Certificate`.

```
/// Cryptographic signature verification: returns true if certificate was signed by issuer
#[cfg(feature = "verify")]
pub fn check_signature(cert: &X509Certificate<'_>, issuer: &X509Certificate<'_>) -> bool {
    let issuer_public_key = issuer.public_key();
    cert
        .verify_signature(Some(issuer_public_key))
        .is_ok()
}
```
- The `validate`features add methods to run more validation functions on the certificate structure and values using the`Validate``verify`above).

[§](https://docs.rs#rust-version-requirements)Rust version requirements

`x509-parser` requires **Rustc version 1.67.1 or greater**, based on der-parser
dependencies and for proc-macro attributes support.

# nix - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/nix/^0.30.1/

**Unix**only.

## Expand description

Rust friendly bindings to the various *nix system functions.

Modules are structured according to the C header file that they would be defined in.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

Nix uses the following Cargo features to enable optional functionality. They may be enabled in any combination.

- `acct`- Process accounting
- `aio`- POSIX AIO
- `dir`- Stuff relating to directory iteration
- `env`- Manipulate environment variables
- `event`- Event-driven APIs, like- `kqueue`and- `epoll`

- `feature`- Query characteristics of the OS at runtime
- `fs`- File system functionality
- `hostname`- Get and set the system’s hostname
- `inotify`- Linux’s- `inotify`file system notification API
- `ioctl`- The- `ioctl`syscall, and wrappers for many specific instances
- `kmod`- Load and unload kernel modules
- `mman`- Stuff relating to memory management
- `mount`- Mount and unmount file systems
- `mqueue`- POSIX message queues
- `net`- Networking-related functionality
- `personality`- Set the process execution domain
- `poll`- APIs like- `poll`and- `select`
- `process`- Stuff relating to running processes
- `pthread`- POSIX threads
- `ptrace`- Process tracing and debugging
- `quota`- File system quotas
- `reboot`- Reboot the system

- `sched`- Manipulate process’s scheduling
- `socket`- Sockets, whether for networking or local use

- `syslog`- System logging

# poem - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/poem/latest/target-redirect/poem/

## Expand description

Poem is a full-featured and easy-to-use web framework with the Rust programming language.

[§](https://docs.rs#table-of-contents)Table of contents

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use poem::{IntoResponse, Route, Server, get, handler, listener::TcpListener, web::Path};
#[handler]
fn hello(Path(name): Path<String>) -> String {
    format!("hello: {}", name)
}
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), std::io::Error> {
    let app = Route::new().at("/hello/:name", get(hello));
    Server::new(TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:3000"))
        .run(app)
        .await
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#endpoint)Endpoint

The [ Endpoint](https://docs.rs/endpoint/trait.Endpoint.html) trait represents a type that can handle HTTP requests, and
it returns a

`Result<T: IntoResponse, Error>` type.The [ handler](https://docs.rs/attr.handler.html) macro is used to convert a function into an endpoint.

```
use poem::{
    Endpoint, Request, Result, error::NotFoundError, handler, http::StatusCode,
    test::TestClient,
};
#[handler]
fn return_str() -> &'static str {
    "hello"
}
#[handler]
fn return_err() -> Result<&'static str, NotFoundError> {
    Err(NotFoundError)
}
let resp = TestClient::new(return_str).get("/").send().await;
resp.assert_status_is_ok();
resp.assert_text("hello").await;
let resp = TestClient::new(return_err).get("/").send().await;
resp.assert_status(StatusCode::NOT_FOUND);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#extractors)Extractors

The extractor is used to extract something from the HTTP request.

`Poem` provides some [commonly used extractors](https://docs.rs/web/trait.FromRequest.html) for
extracting something from HTTP requests.

In the following example, the `index` function uses 3 extractors to extract
the remote address, HTTP method and URI.

```
use poem::{
    handler,
    http::{Method, Uri},
    web::RemoteAddr,
};
#[handler]
fn index(remote_addr: &RemoteAddr, method: Method, uri: &Uri) {}
```
By default, the extractor will return a `400 Bad Request` when an error
occurs, but sometimes you may want to change this behavior, so you can
handle the error yourself.

In the following example, when the [ Query](https://docs.rs/web/struct.Query.html) extractor fails, it
will return a

`500 Internal Server` response and the reason for the error.```
use poem::{
    IntoResponse, Response, Result, error::ParseQueryError, handler, http::StatusCode,
    web::Query,
};
use serde::Deserialize;
#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
struct Params {
    name: String,
}
#[handler]
fn index(res: Result<Query<Params>>) -> Result<impl IntoResponse> {
    match res {
        Ok(Query(params)) => Ok(params.name.into_response()),
        Err(err) if err.is::<ParseQueryError>() => Ok(Response::builder()
            .status(StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)
            .body(err.to_string())),
        Err(err) => Err(err),
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#routing)Routing

There are three available routes.

- `Route`
- `RouteDomain`
- `RouteMethod`

```
use poem::{Route, get, handler, post, web::Path};
#[handler]
async fn get_user(id: Path<String>) {}
#[handler]
async fn delete_user(id: Path<String>) {}
#[handler]
async fn create_user() {}
let app = Route::new()
    .at("/user/:id", get(get_user).delete(delete_user))
    .at("/user", post(create_user));
```
You can create custom extractors, see also [ FromRequest](https://docs.rs/web/trait.FromRequest.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#responses)Responses

All types that can be converted to HTTP response [ Response](https://docs.rs/struct.Response.html) should
implement

[.](https://docs.rs/web/trait.IntoResponse.html)

`IntoResponse`In the following example, the `string_response` and `status_response`
functions return the `String` and `StatusCode` types, because `Poem` has
implemented the [ IntoResponse](https://docs.rs/web/trait.IntoResponse.html) trait for them.

The `no_response` function does not return a value. We can think that
its return type is `()`, and `Poem` also implements [ IntoResponse](https://docs.rs/web/trait.IntoResponse.html) for

`()`, which is always converted to `200 OK`.The `result_response` function returns a `Result` type, which means that an
error may occur.

```
use poem::{Result, handler, http::StatusCode};
#[handler]
fn string_response() -> String {
    todo!()
}
#[handler]
fn status_response() -> StatusCode {
    todo!()
}
#[handler]
fn no_response() {}
#[handler]
fn result_response() -> Result<String> {
    todo!()
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#handling-errors)Handling errors

The following example returns customized content when
[ NotFoundError](https://docs.rs/error/struct.NotFoundError.html) occurs.

```
use poem::{
    EndpointExt, IntoResponse, Response, Route, error::NotFoundError, handler, http::StatusCode,
};
#[handler]
fn foo() {}
#[handler]
fn bar() {}
let app =
    Route::new()
        .at("/foo", foo)
        .at("/bar", bar)
        .catch_error(|err: NotFoundError| async move {
            Response::builder()
                .status(StatusCode::NOT_FOUND)
                .body("custom not found")
        });
```
[§](https://docs.rs#middleware)Middleware

You can call the [ with](https://docs.rs/endpoint/trait.EndpointExt.html#method.with) method on the

[to apply a middleware to an endpoint. It actually converts the original endpoint to a new endpoint.](https://docs.rs/endpoint/trait.Endpoint.html)

`Endpoint````
use poem::{EndpointExt, Route, handler, middleware::Tracing};
#[handler]
fn index() {}
let app = Route::new().at("/", index).with(Tracing);
```
You can create your own middleware, see also [ Middleware](https://docs.rs/middleware/trait.Middleware.html).

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# bamboo_subagent - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bamboo-subagent/2026.7.3/bamboo_subagent/

## Expand description

`bamboo-subagent` — sub-agent fleet runtime.

Slice 1 (this build): pure filesystem logic, no runtime dependency.

- `store`
- `mailbox`

See `docs/subagent-actor-runtime-design.md` (§3.4, §5) and
`docs/subagent-store-mailbox-interface.md` for the design these implement.

The session payload is kept opaque (generic `T: Serialize`/`DeserializeOwned`) so this
crate stays a leaf and is fully unit-testable with a tempdir; higher layers pass the
domain `Session`. Index rebuild is decoupled via the [ store::MetaExtractor](https://docs.rs/store/trait.MetaExtractor.html) seam.

# ikigai_rdf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ikigai-rdf/0.1.3/ikigai_rdf/

## Expand description

`ikigai-rdf` — RDF **transreption** as an ikigai resource.

`urn:rdf:transrept` takes an RDF document and re-serializes it into another syntax,
chosen by the `as` argument (content negotiation): Turtle, N-Triples, N-Quads, TriG,
RDF/XML, JSON-LD, or a human-readable HTML table. The input syntax is sniffed (an
explicit format isn’t needed for the common cases).

It’s the first step toward NetKernel-style *transreption* — lossless transformation
between representations of the same resource. Built on Oxigraph’s **pure** parser/
serializer crates (`oxrdfio`/`oxrdf`) — no store, no rocksdb — so it compiles to
`wasm32` and the browser can transrept a fetched graph **client-side**:

`source urn:httpGet url=https://example.org/thing | urn:rdf:transrept as=text/turtle`The kernel pipes the fetched bytes into `content`; `as` picks the representation.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [space](https://docs.rs/fn.space.html)
- [subclass_](https://docs.rs/fn.subclass_axioms.html)- axioms
- Parse a Turtle alignment graph and return every `rdfs:subClassOf`axiom as a`(subclass, superclass)`IRI pair — the closure pairs a host feeds to the kernel’s type-aware action selection (`Kernel::with_subclass_axioms`), so an entity typed`foaf:Person`satisfies a`schema:Person`action. Best-effort: triples whose subject or object isn’t an IRI (blank nodes, literals) and any unparseable triples are skipped —`subClassOf`relates named classes.

# ikigai_org - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/ikigai-org/0.1.0/ikigai_org/

## Expand description

`ikigai-org` — the org-mode agenda as ROC resources.

`urn:org:agenda:{period}` reads **date-fixed events** (headlines with active
`<…>` timestamps, repeaters expanded into the window) from org files and
serves them as text or as the **same skolemized Turtle event graph**
`urn:personal:calendar` speaks — so org and native calendars union and diff
as graphs (the Brian-Busy materialized-view plan).

The org files are read **through the kernel**: the host binds them (e.g. an
`ikigai-fs` space jailed to the org directory at `urn:orgfile:{path}`) and
hands this space their IRIs. That keeps this crate free of filesystem
access — capability-gated, wasm-clean, and golden-thread-ready when the
host’s file space is cacheable.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-parsed-v1)What is parsed (v1)

Headlines (`* Title`) whose section carries an active timestamp:
`<YYYY-MM-DD [Day] [HH:MM[-HH:MM]] [+N{d,w,m,y}]>`. Inactive `[…]`
timestamps are ignored. Untimed stamps are all-day; a timed stamp without
an end defaults to one hour. Repeaters (`+1w`, `+1y`, …) are expanded into
the requested window.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Agenda](https://docs.rs/struct.AgendaEndpoint.html)- Endpoint
- `urn:org:agenda[:{period}]`— the org agenda for a period (default- `week`), sourced through the kernel from the configured org-file resources.
- [OrgEvent](https://docs.rs/struct.OrgEvent.html)
- One agenda event, normalized. The same shape the calendar side speaks.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [agenda_](https://docs.rs/fn.agenda_events.html)- events
- Parse org text into the events overlapping `[win_start, win_end)`, expanding repeaters into the window.
- [space](https://docs.rs/fn.space.html)
- Mount the agenda: `urn:org:agenda`and`urn:org:agenda:{period}`, reading the given org-file resources through the kernel.

# pdfmuse_core - Rust

pdfmuse-core — deterministic PDF/DOCX parser core.

- Unified intermediate representation (IR).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Chunk](https://docs.rs/struct.Chunk.html)
- A retrieval unit: a block’s text plus the context needed to cite it.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [chunk](https://docs.rs/fn.chunk.html)
- Split `doc`into chunks (one per non-empty block), tracking heading context.
- [parse](https://docs.rs/fn.parse.html)
- Parse `data`into the unified`ir::Document`
- [parse_](https://docs.rs/fn.parse_with_password.html)- with_ - password
- Like `parse``password`for encrypted PDFs.
- [to_json](https://docs.rs/fn.to_json.html)
- Serialize the entire `Document`
- [to_](https://docs.rs/fn.to_markdown.html)- markdown
- Render `doc`to GitHub-flavored Markdown, pages and blocks in order.
- [to_text](https://docs.rs/fn.to_text.html)
- Render `doc`to plain reading-order text — no Markdown syntax, just the block text joined by newlines. The cheapest useful output for search / ATS / feeding an LLM, and (via the bindings) avoids materializing the full IR on the host.

# facett_tabbar - Rust

## Expand description

**facett-tabbar** — the generic, themed **nav toolbar**: a control strip
(workspace/palette/About/live-style pickers + toggles, host-painted) plus a
two-row strip of tab headers, the active tab carrying the palette accent.
Adopted from nornir’s `src/viz/facett_ui.rs` (`TabBar` / `TabItem` /
`BarControl`) — the header of that file explicitly says it “should live in
the upstream `facett` crate”; the only thing that kept it in nornir is the
egui 0.33↔0.34 skew (egui-snarl pins 0.33). facett is on egui 0.34, so this
is the re-home; nornir re-points to `facett::tabbar::TabBar` once its viz
bumps to 0.34 (still gated on egui-snarl shipping 0.34 — see the cut policy
note in the batch report).

Two surfaces:

- `TabBar`- `&[TabItem]`+ an- `active`id), the verbatim port of nornir’s bar.- `show()`returns the id of the newly-clicked tab;- `state_json()`reports the tabs/active/split/controls.
- `TabBarView`- **owning**canonical- `Facet`- `local()`/- `remote()`,- `state_json()`,- `caps()`) so a- `FacetDeck`mounts the bar as a tab and a headless driver reads + drives the selection. It tracks its own- `active`and clicking a header re-keys it (and records the click count).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [BarControl](https://docs.rs/struct.BarControl.html)
- A declarative descriptor of one **picker / toggle / button**the bar hosts in its left/right slots (workspace combo, palette combo, About toggle, live checkbox, …). The bar does NOT paint these — the host paints them through a slot closure — but the descriptor lets`state_json`report*which*controls are present and their values (the “components expose readable data” LAW) without the bar knowing anything domain-specific.
- [TabBar](https://docs.rs/struct.TabBar.html)
- The generic, themed **nav/toolbar**widget: a control strip plus a two-row strip of tab headers, all painted in the active`Theme``&[TabItem]`, the left/right slots are host-supplied closures, and the controls they host are declared as`BarControl`
- [TabBar](https://docs.rs/struct.TabBarView.html)- View
- An **owning**canonical`Facet``TabBar``tabs`+`active`+`controls`, paints the bar (no host slots — the controls are reported, not interactive here), tracks the live selection across frames, and exposes the whole rendered bar through`Facet::state_json`
- [TabItem](https://docs.rs/struct.TabItem.html)
- One tab in a `TabBar``id`(emitted in`state_json`+ matched on click) plus the human`label`egui paints on the header (icon + words, e.g.`"🔗 Dep Graph"`), so an AccessKit/robot click resolves by the same string the user reads. Keeping`id`and`label`separate lets a host rename a label without breaking click-by-id wiring or the`state_json`contract.
- [Underline](https://docs.rs/struct.UnderlineTween.html)- Tween
- Active-tab **underline slide**state (injected-clock, FC-7): holds the current eased underline rect, which each frame eases toward the active tab’s rect. Held by the owning`TabBarView``TabBar::show_anim`

# facett_plotters - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/facett-plotters/0.1.10/facett_plotters/

## Expand description

**facett-plotters** — the chart types [ egui_plot](https://docs.rs/egui_plot)
(→

`facett-plot`) *lacks*, painted in

**immediate mode**directly on an

[.](https://docs.rs/egui/0.34.3/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/egui/painter/struct.Painter.html)

`egui::Painter``egui_plot` already covers line/scatter/bar/histogram with
zoom/pan; this crate fills the analytics long-tail Plotly defines:- `BoxPlotView`
- `ViolinView`
- `HeatmapView`
- `CandlestickView`
- `TreemapView`

[§](https://docs.rs#why-hand-rolled-not-the-plotters-crate)Why hand-rolled, not the `plotters` crate

The `plotters` crate is **retained + raster/SVG-backend driven**: its egui
integration renders to a bitmap and blits a texture every frame, with no
immediate-mode hit-testing, no live theming, and no hover model. facett’s
charts must read [`facett_core::theme`] live (re-skin on theme switch),
expose cheap hover-readouts, and implement the [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html)
contract (

`caps()` + `copy()` → CSV). Hand-painting on the egui `Painter`
(the same path `facett-core`/`facett-map` use) is the lighter, better-fitting
choice — so `plotters` is *not*a dependency.

[§](https://docs.rs#theme-derived-colour-ramps)Theme-derived colour ramps

No palette is hardcoded. [ ramp::Ramp](https://docs.rs/ramp/struct.Ramp.html) builds a

**sequential**(

`bg`→`accent`→`glow`) or **diverging**(

`accent`→`text_dim`→`glow`) ramp
purely from the active [, so heatmaps/treemaps follow whatever theme is set.](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/theme/struct.Theme.html)

`Theme`Each view is a [ Facet](https://docs.rs/facett-core/0.1.10/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/facett_core/trait.Facet.html): it declares

`caps().themeable().copyable().resizable()`, paints itself, and `copy()`
emits the underlying data as CSV. The data→geometry math (quartiles, KDE
bins, OHLC mapping, heatmap cell layout, treemap squarify) lives in **pure, tested functions**that need no GPU.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use boxplot::`- [BoxPlotView](https://docs.rs/boxplot/struct.BoxPlotView.html);
- `pub use boxplot::`- [Quartiles](https://docs.rs/boxplot/struct.Quartiles.html);
- `pub use candlestick::`- [CandlestickView](https://docs.rs/candlestick/struct.CandlestickView.html);
- `pub use candlestick::`- [Ohlc](https://docs.rs/candlestick/struct.Ohlc.html);
- `pub use candlestick::`- [OhlcLayout](https://docs.rs/candlestick/struct.OhlcLayout.html);
- `pub use heatmap::`- [HeatmapView](https://docs.rs/heatmap/struct.HeatmapView.html);
- `pub use ramp::`- [Ramp](https://docs.rs/ramp/struct.Ramp.html);
- `pub use treemap::`- [Tile](https://docs.rs/treemap/struct.Tile.html);
- `pub use treemap::`- [TreemapView](https://docs.rs/treemap/struct.TreemapView.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [boxplot](https://docs.rs/boxplot/index.html)
- **Box plot**— quartiles + whiskers + outliers, one box per named group. The data→geometry math (- `Quartiles::from_sorted`- `Quartiles::compute`- `BoxPlotView`- `Facet`
- [candlestick](https://docs.rs/candlestick/index.html)

- [heatmap](https://docs.rs/heatmap/index.html)

- **Theme-derived colour ramps.**No hardcoded palette: a sequential ramp is built from the theme’s- `bg`→- `accent`→- `glow`, and a diverging ramp from- `accent`(low) through a neutral midpoint to- `glow`(high). Charts call- `Ramp::at`- `t ∈ 0..=1`to map a scalar to a colour.
- [treemap](https://docs.rs/treemap/index.html)
- **Treemap**— weighted rectangles, area ∝ value, laid out by a deterministic- **slice-and-dice**algorithm that alternates split direction by depth-of-cut so the tiling stays readable. The layout (- `squarify`- `(index, Rect)`pairs, tested independently of any painter. Tile fills come from a theme-derived sequential- `Ramp`
- [violin](https://docs.rs/violin/index.html)
- **Violin plot**— a mirrored kernel-density silhouette per group. The KDE (- `kde`- `ViolinView`

# poem 3.1.12 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/poem/3.1.12

## Features

- Both *Ease*of use and performance.
- Minimizing the use of generics.
- Blazing fast and flexible routing.
- `tower::Service`and- `tower::Layer`compatibility.
- Use [poem-openapi](https://crates.io/crates/poem-openapi)to write APIs that comply with[OAS3](https://github.com/OAI/OpenAPI-Specification)specifications and automatically generate documents.

## Crate features

To avoid compiling unused dependencies, Poem gates certain features, all of which are disabled by default:

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| server | Server and listener APIs (enabled by default) |
| compression | Support decompress request body and compress response body |
| cookie | Support for Cookie |
| csrf | Support for Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) protection |
| multipart | Support for Multipart |
| native-tls | Support for HTTP server over TLS with `native-tls` |
| openssl-tls | Support for HTTP server over TLS with `openssl-tls` |
| opentelemetry | Support for opentelemetry |
| prometheus | Support for Prometheus |
| redis-session | Support for RedisSession |
| rustls | Support for HTTP server over TLS with `rustls` |
| session | Support for session |
| sse | Support Server-Sent Events (SSE) |
| static-files | Support static files endpoint |
| tempfile | Support for `tempfile` |
| tower-compat | Adapters for `tower::Layer`and`tower::Service`. |
| websocket | Support for WebSocket |
| anyhow | Integrate with crate.`anyhow` |
| eyre06 | Integrate with version 0.6.x of the crate.`eyre` |
| i18n | Support for internationalization |
| acme-native-roots | Support for ACME(Automatic Certificate Management Environment) |
| acme-webpki-roots | Support for ACME using webpki TLS roots rather than native TLS roots |
| tokio-metrics | Integrate with crate.`tokio-metrics` |
| embed | Integrate with crate.`rust-embed` |
| xml | Integrate with crate.`quick-xml` |
| yaml | Integrate with crate.`serde-yaml` |
| requestid | Associates an unique ID with each incoming request |
| sonic-rs | Uses instead of`sonic-rs``serde_json`. Pls, checkout`sonic-rs`requirements to properly enable`sonic-rs`capabilities |

This crate uses `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` to ensure everything is implemented in 100% Safe Rust.

# poem - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/poem/3.1.12/target-redirect/poem/

## Expand description

Poem is a full-featured and easy-to-use web framework with the Rust programming language.

[§](https://docs.rs#table-of-contents)Table of contents

[§](https://docs.rs#quickstart)Quickstart

```
use poem::{IntoResponse, Route, Server, get, handler, listener::TcpListener, web::Path};
#[handler]
fn hello(Path(name): Path<String>) -> String {
    format!("hello: {}", name)
}
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), std::io::Error> {
    let app = Route::new().at("/hello/:name", get(hello));
    Server::new(TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:3000"))
        .run(app)
        .await
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#endpoint)Endpoint

The [ Endpoint](https://docs.rs/endpoint/trait.Endpoint.html) trait represents a type that can handle HTTP requests, and
it returns a

`Result<T: IntoResponse, Error>` type.The [ handler](https://docs.rs/attr.handler.html) macro is used to convert a function into an endpoint.

```
use poem::{
    Endpoint, Request, Result, error::NotFoundError, handler, http::StatusCode,
    test::TestClient,
};
#[handler]
fn return_str() -> &'static str {
    "hello"
}
#[handler]
fn return_err() -> Result<&'static str, NotFoundError> {
    Err(NotFoundError)
}
let resp = TestClient::new(return_str).get("/").send().await;
resp.assert_status_is_ok();
resp.assert_text("hello").await;
let resp = TestClient::new(return_err).get("/").send().await;
resp.assert_status(StatusCode::NOT_FOUND);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#extractors)Extractors

The extractor is used to extract something from the HTTP request.

`Poem` provides some [commonly used extractors](https://docs.rs/web/trait.FromRequest.html) for
extracting something from HTTP requests.

In the following example, the `index` function uses 3 extractors to extract
the remote address, HTTP method and URI.

```
use poem::{
    handler,
    http::{Method, Uri},
    web::RemoteAddr,
};
#[handler]
fn index(remote_addr: &RemoteAddr, method: Method, uri: &Uri) {}
```
By default, the extractor will return a `400 Bad Request` when an error
occurs, but sometimes you may want to change this behavior, so you can
handle the error yourself.

In the following example, when the [ Query](https://docs.rs/web/struct.Query.html) extractor fails, it
will return a

`500 Internal Server` response and the reason for the error.```
use poem::{
    IntoResponse, Response, Result, error::ParseQueryError, handler, http::StatusCode,
    web::Query,
};
use serde::Deserialize;
#[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
struct Params {
    name: String,
}
#[handler]
fn index(res: Result<Query<Params>>) -> Result<impl IntoResponse> {
    match res {
        Ok(Query(params)) => Ok(params.name.into_response()),
        Err(err) if err.is::<ParseQueryError>() => Ok(Response::builder()
            .status(StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)
            .body(err.to_string())),
        Err(err) => Err(err),
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#routing)Routing

There are three available routes.

- `Route`
- `RouteDomain`
- `RouteMethod`

```
use poem::{Route, get, handler, post, web::Path};
#[handler]
async fn get_user(id: Path<String>) {}
#[handler]
async fn delete_user(id: Path<String>) {}
#[handler]
async fn create_user() {}
let app = Route::new()
    .at("/user/:id", get(get_user).delete(delete_user))
    .at("/user", post(create_user));
```
You can create custom extractors, see also [ FromRequest](https://docs.rs/web/trait.FromRequest.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#responses)Responses

All types that can be converted to HTTP response [ Response](https://docs.rs/struct.Response.html) should
implement

[.](https://docs.rs/web/trait.IntoResponse.html)

`IntoResponse`In the following example, the `string_response` and `status_response`
functions return the `String` and `StatusCode` types, because `Poem` has
implemented the [ IntoResponse](https://docs.rs/web/trait.IntoResponse.html) trait for them.

The `no_response` function does not return a value. We can think that
its return type is `()`, and `Poem` also implements [ IntoResponse](https://docs.rs/web/trait.IntoResponse.html) for

`()`, which is always converted to `200 OK`.The `result_response` function returns a `Result` type, which means that an
error may occur.

```
use poem::{Result, handler, http::StatusCode};
#[handler]
fn string_response() -> String {
    todo!()
}
#[handler]
fn status_response() -> StatusCode {
    todo!()
}
#[handler]
fn no_response() {}
#[handler]
fn result_response() -> Result<String> {
    todo!()
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#handling-errors)Handling errors

The following example returns customized content when
[ NotFoundError](https://docs.rs/error/struct.NotFoundError.html) occurs.

```
use poem::{
    EndpointExt, IntoResponse, Response, Route, error::NotFoundError, handler, http::StatusCode,
};
#[handler]
fn foo() {}
#[handler]
fn bar() {}
let app =
    Route::new()
        .at("/foo", foo)
        .at("/bar", bar)
        .catch_error(|err: NotFoundError| async move {
            Response::builder()
                .status(StatusCode::NOT_FOUND)
                .body("custom not found")
        });
```
[§](https://docs.rs#middleware)Middleware

You can call the [ with](https://docs.rs/endpoint/trait.EndpointExt.html#method.with) method on the

[to apply a middleware to an endpoint. It actually converts the original endpoint to a new endpoint.](https://docs.rs/endpoint/trait.Endpoint.html)

`Endpoint````
use poem::{EndpointExt, Route, handler, middleware::Tracing};
#[handler]
fn index() {}
let app = Route::new().at("/", index).with(Tracing);
```
You can create your own middleware, see also [ Middleware](https://docs.rs/middleware/trait.Middleware.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#crate-features)Crate features

To avoid compiling unused dependencies, `Poem` gates certain features, all
of which are disabled by default:

| Feature | Description |
|---|---|
| server | Server and listener APIs(enable by default) |
| compression | Support decompress request body and compress response body |
| cookie | Support for Cookie |
| csrf | Support for Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) protection |
| multipart | Support for Multipart |
| native-tls | Support for HTTP server over TLS with `native-tls` |
| openssl-tls | Support for HTTP server over TLS with `openssl-tls` |
| opentelemetry | Support for opentelemetry |
| prometheus | Support for Prometheus |
| redis-session | Support for RedisSession |
| rustls | Support for HTTP server over TLS with `rustls` |
| session | Support for session |
| sse | Support Server-Sent Events (SSE) |
| tempfile | Support for `tempfile` |
| test | Test utilities to test your endpoints. |
| tower-compat | Adapters for `tower::Layer`and`tower::Service`. |
| websocket | Support for WebSocket |
| anyhow | Integrate with the crate.`anyhow` |
| eyre06 | Integrate with version 0.6.x of the crate.`eyre` |
| i18n | Support for internationalization |
| acme-native-roots | Support for ACME(Automatic Certificate Management Environment) |
| acme-webpki-roots | Support for ACME using webpki TLS roots rather than native TLS roots |
| tokio-metrics | Integrate with the crate.`tokio-metrics` |
| embed | Integrate with crate.`rust-embed` |
| xml | Integrate with crate.`quick-xml` |
| yaml | Integrate with crate.`serde-yaml` |
| sonic-rs | Uses instead of`sonic-rs``serde_json`. Pls, checkout`sonic-rs`requirements to properly enable`sonic-rs`capabilities |

- A helper function, similar to `RouteMethod::new().patch(ep)`.
- [post](https://docs.rs/fn.post.html)
- A helper function, similar to `RouteMethod::new().post(ep)`.
- [put](https://docs.rs/fn.put.html)
- A helper function, similar to `RouteMethod::new().put(ep)`.
- [trace](https://docs.rs/fn.trace.html)
- A helper function, similar to `RouteMethod::new().trace(ep)`.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [handler](https://docs.rs/attr.handler.html)
- Wrap an asynchronous function as an `Endpoint`.

# lib.rs - source

Source: https://docs.rs/poem/3.1.12/src/poem/lib.rs.html

# poem/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! Poem is a full-featured and easy-to-use web framework with the Rust
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! programming language.
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//!
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! # Table of contents
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//!
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! - [Quickstart](#quickstart)
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! - [Endpoint](#endpoint)
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//! - [Extractors](#extractors)
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! - [Routing](#routing)
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! - [Responses](#responses)
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! - [Handling errors](#handling-errors)
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! - [Middleware](#middleware)
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! - [Crate features](#crate-features)
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//!
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//! # Quickstart
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//!
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! ```no_run
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//! use poem::{IntoResponse, Route, Server, get, handler, listener::TcpListener, web::Path};
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//!
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//! #[handler]
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//! fn hello(Path(name): Path<String>) -> String {
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!     format!("hello: {}", name)
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//! }
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//!
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//! #[tokio::main]
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! async fn main() -> Result<(), std::io::Error> {
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//!     let app = Route::new().at("/hello/:name", get(hello));
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//!     Server::new(TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:3000"))
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//!         .run(app)
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//!         .await
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! }
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//! ```
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//! # Endpoint
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//! The [`Endpoint`] trait represents a type that can handle HTTP requests, and
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//! it returns a `Result<T: IntoResponse, Error>` type.
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//! The [`handler`] macro is used to convert a function into an endpoint.
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! ```
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//! use poem::{
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//!     Endpoint, Request, Result, error::NotFoundError, handler, http::StatusCode,
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//!     test::TestClient,
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! };
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! #[handler]
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! fn return_str() -> &'static str {
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!     "hello"
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! }
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//!
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//! #[handler]
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! fn return_err() -> Result<&'static str, NotFoundError> {
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//!     Err(NotFoundError)
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! }
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//!
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! # tokio::runtime::Runtime::new().unwrap().block_on(async {
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! let resp = TestClient::new(return_str).get("/").send().await;
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! resp.assert_status_is_ok();
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! resp.assert_text("hello").await;
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//!
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//! let resp = TestClient::new(return_err).get("/").send().await;
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! resp.assert_status(StatusCode::NOT_FOUND);
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! # });
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! ```
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//!
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//! # Extractors
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//!
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! The extractor is used to extract something from the HTTP request.
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! `Poem` provides some [commonly used extractors](web::FromRequest) for
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! extracting something from HTTP requests.
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! In the following example, the `index` function uses 3 extractors to extract
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! the remote address, HTTP method and URI.
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//!
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! ```
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! use poem::{
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!     handler,
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//!     http::{Method, Uri},
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//!     web::RemoteAddr,
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! };
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//!
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//! #[handler]
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! fn index(remote_addr: &RemoteAddr, method: Method, uri: &Uri) {}
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! ```
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//!
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//! By default, the extractor will return a `400 Bad Request` when an error
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! occurs, but sometimes you may want to change this behavior, so you can
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//! handle the error yourself.
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//!
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//! In the following example, when the [`Query`](web::Query) extractor fails, it
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! will return a `500 Internal Server` response and the reason for the error.
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//!
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! ```
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//! use poem::{
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//!     IntoResponse, Response, Result, error::ParseQueryError, handler, http::StatusCode,
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//!     web::Query,
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! };
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! use serde::Deserialize;
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//!
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//! #[derive(Debug, Deserialize)]
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! struct Params {
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//!     name: String,
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! }
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//!
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//! #[handler]
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! fn index(res: Result<Query<Params>>) -> Result<impl IntoResponse> {
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//!     match res {
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//!         Ok(Query(params)) => Ok(params.name.into_response()),
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//!         Err(err) if err.is::<ParseQueryError>() => Ok(Response::builder()
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//!             .status(StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//!             .body(err.to_string())),
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//!         Err(err) => Err(err),
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//!     }
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! }
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//! ```
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//!
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! # Routing
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//!
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! There are three available routes.
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! - [`Route`] Routing for path
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! - [`RouteDomain`] Routing for domain
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! - [`RouteMethod`] Routing for HTTP method
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//!
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//! ```
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! use poem::{Route, get, handler, post, web::Path};
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! #[handler]
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! async fn get_user(id: Path<String>) {}
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//!
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//! #[handler]
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! async fn delete_user(id: Path<String>) {}
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//!
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! #[handler]
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! async fn create_user() {}
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//!
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! let app = Route::new()
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//!     .at("/user/:id", get(get_user).delete(delete_user))
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//!     .at("/user", post(create_user));
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//! ```
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//!
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! You can create custom extractors, see also [`FromRequest`].
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//!
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! # Responses
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//!
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//! All types that can be converted to HTTP response [`Response`] should
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! implement [`IntoResponse`].
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//!
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! In the following example, the `string_response` and `status_response`
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! functions return the `String` and `StatusCode` types, because `Poem` has
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//! implemented the [`IntoResponse`] trait for them.
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//!
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! The `no_response` function does not return a value. We can think that
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! its return type is `()`, and `Poem` also implements [`IntoResponse`] for
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! `()`, which is always converted to `200 OK`.
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//!
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//! The `result_response` function returns a `Result` type, which means that an
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! error may occur.
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! ```
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//! use poem::{Result, handler, http::StatusCode};
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//!
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! #[handler]
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! fn string_response() -> String {
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//!     todo!()
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! }
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//!
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//! #[handler]
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! fn status_response() -> StatusCode {
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//!     todo!()
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! }
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//!
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! #[handler]
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//! fn no_response() {}
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//!
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//! #[handler]
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! fn result_response() -> Result<String> {
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!     todo!()
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! }
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//! ```
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//!
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! # Handling errors
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//!
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! The following example returns customized content when
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! [`NotFoundError`](error::NotFoundError) occurs.
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//!
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! ```
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//! use poem::{
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//!     EndpointExt, IntoResponse, Response, Route, error::NotFoundError, handler, http::StatusCode,
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//! };
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//!
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//! #[handler]
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! fn foo() {}
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//!
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! #[handler]
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! fn bar() {}
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//!
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! let app =
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//!     Route::new()
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//!         .at("/foo", foo)
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//!         .at("/bar", bar)
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//!         .catch_error(|err: NotFoundError| async move {
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//!             Response::builder()
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//!                 .status(StatusCode::NOT_FOUND)
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//!                 .body("custom not found")
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//!         });
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! ```
[209](https://docs.rs#209)//!
[210](https://docs.rs#210)//! # Middleware
[211](https://docs.rs#211)//!
[212](https://docs.rs#212)//! You can call the [`with`](EndpointExt::with) method on the [`Endpoint`] to
[213](https://docs.rs#213)//! apply a middleware to an endpoint. It actually converts the original
[214](https://docs.rs#214)//! endpoint to a new endpoint.
[215](https://docs.rs#215)//! ```
[216](https://docs.rs#216)//! use poem::{EndpointExt, Route, handler, middleware::Tracing};
[217](https://docs.rs#217)//!
[218](https://docs.rs#218)//! #[handler]
[219](https://docs.rs#219)//! fn index() {}
[220](https://docs.rs#220)//!
[221](https://docs.rs#221)//! let app = Route::new().at("/", index).with(Tracing);
[222](https://docs.rs#222)//! ```
[223](https://docs.rs#223)//!
[224](https://docs.rs#224)//! You can create your own middleware, see also [`Middleware`].
[225](https://docs.rs#225)//!

# Endpoint in poem::endpoint - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/poem/3.1.12/poem/endpoint/trait.Endpoint.html

`pub trait Endpoint: `[Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) + [Sync](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sync.html) {
    type [Output](https://docs.rs#associatedtype.Output): [IntoResponse](https://docs.rs/web/trait.IntoResponse.html);
    // Required method
    fn [call](https://docs.rs#tymethod.call)(
        &self,
        req: [Request](https://docs.rs/struct.Request.html),
    ) -> impl [Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html)<Output = [Result](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html)<Self::[Output](https://docs.rs/trait.Endpoint.html#associatedtype.Output)>> + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html);
    // Provided method
    fn [get_response](https://docs.rs#method.get_response)(
        &self,
        req: [Request](https://docs.rs/struct.Request.html),
    ) -> impl [Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html)<Output = [Response](https://docs.rs/struct.Response.html)> + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

An HTTP request handler.

## Required Associated Types[§](https://docs.rs#required-associated-types)

## Required Methods[§](https://docs.rs#required-methods)

## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Get the response to the request and return a [ Response](https://docs.rs/struct.Response.html).

Unlike [ Endpoint::call](https://docs.rs/trait.Endpoint.html#tymethod.call), when an error occurs, it will also convert
the error into a response object.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use poem::{
    Endpoint, Request, Result, error::NotFoundError, handler, http::StatusCode,
    test::TestClient,
};
#[handler]
fn index() -> Result<()> {
    Err(NotFoundError.into())
}
TestClient::new(index)
    .get("/")
    .send()
    .await
    .assert_status(StatusCode::NOT_FOUND);
```
## Dyn Compatibility[§](https://docs.rs#dyn-compatibility)

This trait is **not** [dyn compatible](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/reference/items/traits.html#dyn-compatibility).

*In older versions of Rust, dyn compatibility was called "object safety".*

# FromRequest in poem::web - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/poem/3.1.12/poem/web/trait.FromRequest.html

`pub trait FromRequest<'a>: `[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) {
    // Required method
    fn [from_request](https://docs.rs#tymethod.from_request)(
        req: &'a [Request](https://docs.rs/struct.Request.html),
        body: &mut [RequestBody](https://docs.rs/struct.RequestBody.html),
    ) -> impl [Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html)<Output = [Result](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html)<Self>> + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html);
    // Provided method
    fn [from_request_without_body](https://docs.rs#method.from_request_without_body)(
        req: &'a [Request](https://docs.rs/struct.Request.html),
    ) -> impl [Future](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/future/future/trait.Future.html)<Output = [Result](https://docs.rs/error/type.Result.html)<Self>> + [Send](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Send.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

Represents an type that can be extract from requests.

[§](https://docs.rs#provided-implementations)Provided Implementations

-
**Option<T>**Extracts `T`from the incoming request, returns`None`
-
**&Request**Extracts the `Request`
-
**&RemoteAddr**Extracts the remote peer’s address `RemoteAddr`
-
**&LocalAddr**Extracts the local server’s address `LocalAddr`
-
**RealIp**Extracts the remote peer’s real ip address from request.
-
**Method**Extracts the `Method`
-
**Version**Extracts the `Version`
-
**&Uri**Extracts the `Uri`
-
**&HeaderMap**Extracts the `HeaderMap`
-
**Data<&T>**Extracts the `Data`
-
**TypedHeader<T>**Extracts the `TypedHeader`
-
**Path<T>**Extracts the `Path`
-
**Query<T>**Extracts the `Query`
-
**Form<T>**Extracts the `Form`
-
**Json<T>**Extracts the `Json`*This extractor will take over the requested body, so you should avoid using multiple extractors of this type in one handler.*
-
**Xml<T>**Extracts the `Xml`*This extractor will take over the requested body, so you should avoid using multiple extractors of this type in one handler.*
-
**TempFile**Extracts the `TempFile`*This extractor will take over the requested body, so you should avoid using multiple extractors of this type in one handler.*
-
**Multipart**Extracts the `Multipart`*This extractor will take over the requested body, so you should avoid using multiple extractors of this type in one handler.*
-
**&CookieJar**Extracts the `CookieJar`*Requires*`CookieJarManager`middleware.
-
**&Session**Extracts the `Session`*Requires*`CookieSession`or`RedisSession`middleware.
-
**Body**Extracts the `Body`*This extractor will take over the requested body, so you should avoid using multiple extractors of this type in one handler.*
-
**String**Extracts the body from the incoming request and parse it into utf8 `String`*This extractor will take over the requested body, so you should avoid using multiple extractors of this type in one handler.*
-
**Vec<u8>**Extracts the body from the incoming request and collect it into `Vec<u8>`*This extractor will take over the requested body, so you should avoid using multiple extractors of this type in one handler.*
-
**Bytes**Extracts the body from the incoming request and collect it into `Bytes`*This extractor will take over the requested body, so you should avoid using multiple extractors of this type in one handler.*
-
**WebSocket**Ready to accept a websocket `WebSocket`
-
**Locale**Extracts the `Locale`
-
**StaticFileRequest**Ready to accept a static file request `StaticFileRequest`
-
**Accept**Extracts the `Accept`header from the incoming request.
-
**PathPattern**Extracts the matched path pattern from the incoming request.

[§](https://docs.rs#create-your-own-extractor)Create your own extractor

The following is an example of a custom token extractor, which extracts the
token from the `MyToken` header.

```
use std::fmt::{self, Display, Formatter};
use poem::{
    Endpoint, Error, FromRequest, Request, RequestBody, Result, Route, get, handler,
    http::StatusCode, test::TestClient,
};
struct Token(String);
impl<'a> FromRequest<'a> for Token {
    async fn from_request(req: &'a Request, body: &mut RequestBody) -> Result<Self> {
        let token = req
            .headers()
            .get("MyToken")
            .and_then(|value| value.to_str().ok())
            .ok_or_else(|| Error::from_string("missing token", StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST))?;
        Ok(Token(token.to_string()))
    }
}
#[handler]
async fn index(token: Token) {
    assert_eq!(token.0, "token123");
}
let app = Route::new().at("/", get(index));
let cli = TestClient::new(app);
cli.get("/")
    .header("MyToken", "token123")
    .send()
    .await
    .assert_status_is_ok();
```

# Query in poem::web - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/poem/3.1.12/poem/web/struct.Query.html

`pub struct Query<T>(pub T);`## Expand description

An extractor that can deserialize some type from query string.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use poem::{
    Endpoint, Request, Route, get, handler,
    http::{Method, StatusCode, Uri},
    test::TestClient,
    web::Query,
};
use serde::Deserialize;
#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct CreateDocument {
    title: String,
    content: String,
}
#[handler]
fn index(Query(CreateDocument { title, content }): Query<CreateDocument>) -> String {
    format!("{}:{}", title, content)
}
let app = Route::new().at("/", get(index).post(index));
let cli = TestClient::new(app);
let resp = cli
    .get("/")
    .query("title", &"foo")
    .query("content", &"bar")
    .send()
    .await;
resp.assert_status_is_ok();
resp.assert_text("foo:bar").await;
```

**crate feature**only.`streams`This is a basic version of making XPENDING command calls which only
passes a stream

`key` and consumer `group` and it
returns details about which consumers have pending messages
that haven’t been acked. DIFF1(X, Y1, Y2, …) (Relative complement difference)

Perform a

Logical representation: ¬X ∧ (Y1 ∨ Y2 ∨ …)

Perform a

**relative complement set difference**to extract the members of one or more of Y1, Y2,… that are not members of X.Logical representation: ¬X ∧ (Y1 ∨ Y2 ∨ …)

[Redis Docs](https://redis.io/commands/BITOP)ONE(X, Y1, Y2, …)

Perform an

Logical representation: (X ∨ Y1 ∨ Y2 ∨ …) ∧ ¬((X ∧ Y1) ∨ (X ∧ Y2) ∨ (Y1 ∧ Y2) ∨ (Y1 ∧ Y3) ∨ …)

Perform an

**“exclusive membership”**operation to extract the members of exactly**one**of X, Y1, Y2, ….Logical representation: (X ∨ Y1 ∨ Y2 ∨ …) ∧ ¬((X ∧ Y1) ∨ (X ∧ Y2) ∨ (Y1 ∧ Y2) ∨ (Y1 ∧ Y3) ∨ …)

#### fn [hexpire](https://docs.rs/redis/0.32.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/redis/commands/trait.TypedCommands.html#method.hexpire)<'a, K, F>(
    &'a mut self,

    seconds: [i64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i64.html),
    opt: [ExpireOption](https://docs.rs/redis/0.32.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/redis/types/enum.ExpireOption.html),
    fields: F,
) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[Vec](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/vec/struct.Vec.html)<[IntegerReplyOrNoOp](https://docs.rs/redis/0.32.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/redis/types/enum.IntegerReplyOrNoOp.html)>, [RedisError](https://docs.rs/redis/0.32.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/redis/types/struct.RedisError.html)>

Set one or more fields’ time to live in seconds.
Returns an array where each element corresponds to the field at the same index in the fields argument.
Each element of the array is either:
0 if the specified condition has not been met.
1 if the expiration time was updated.
2 if called with 0 seconds.
Errors if provided key exists but is not a hash.

configuration option), this command will reload the ACLs from the file,
replacing all the current ACL rules with the ones defined in the file.

`group`. It expects the stream key
to already exist. Otherwise, use `xgroup_create_mkstream` if it doesn’t.

all consumers to read from the last message added to stream. # Route in poem - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/poem/3.1.12/poem/struct.Route.html

`pub struct Route { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

Routing object

You can match the full path or wildcard path, and use the
[ Path](https://docs.rs/web/struct.Path.html) extractor to get the path parameters.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use poem::{
    Endpoint, Request, Route, get, handler,
    http::{StatusCode, Uri},
    test::TestClient,
    web::Path,
};
#[handler]
async fn a() {}
#[handler]
async fn b(Path((group, name)): Path<(String, String)>) {
    assert_eq!(group, "foo");
    assert_eq!(name, "bar");
}
#[handler]
async fn c(Path(path): Path<String>) {
    assert_eq!(path, "d/e");
}
let app = Route::new()
    // full path
    .at("/a/b", get(a))
    // capture parameters
    .at("/b/:group/:name", get(b))
    // capture tail path
    .at("/c/*path", get(c))
    // match regex
    .at("/d/<\\d+>", get(a))
    // capture with regex
    .at("/e/:name<\\d+>", get(a));
let cli = TestClient::new(app);
// /a/b
cli.get("/a/b").send().await.assert_status_is_ok();
// /b/:group/:name
cli.get("/b/foo/bar").send().await.assert_status_is_ok();
// /c/*path
cli.get("/c/d/e").send().await.assert_status_is_ok();
// /d/<\\d>
cli.get("/d/123").send().await.assert_status_is_ok();
// /e/:name<\\d>
cli.get("/e/123").send().await.assert_status_is_ok();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#nested)Nested

```
use poem::{
    Endpoint, Request, Route, handler,
    http::{StatusCode, Uri},
    test::TestClient,
};
#[handler]
fn index() -> &'static str {
    "hello"
}
let app = Route::new().nest("/foo", Route::new().at("/bar", index));
let cli = TestClient::new(app);
let resp = cli.get("/foo/bar").send().await;
resp.assert_status_is_ok();
resp.assert_text("hello").await;
```
[§](https://docs.rs#nested-no-strip)Nested no strip

```
use poem::{
    Endpoint, Request, Route, handler,
    http::{StatusCode, Uri},
    test::TestClient,
};
#[handler]
fn index() -> &'static str {
    "hello"
}
let app = Route::new().nest_no_strip("/foo", Route::new().at("/foo/bar", index));
let cli = TestClient::new(app);
let resp = cli.get("/foo/bar").send().await;
resp.assert_status_is_ok();
resp.assert_text("hello").await;
```

prefix.
